text:
One of the best tells that a technology will change the world: it makes a chaotic entrance.

In the 1980s, employees lied on procurement forms to get PCs into the office, claiming they were buying oscilloscopes or typewriters, while experts warned of "shadow" data processing departments.

Spreadsheets, the original "workplace agent," filled companies with models only their creator could understand.

Email broke the mailroom's control over who could reach whom.

Each time, the fix was a habitat: guardrails that kept the bottom-up energy alive while reining in the chaos just enough.

Now agents are following the same path. As Replit's Amjad Masad puts it, "Today, most agents live somewhere chaotic. They run in chat windows, personal accounts, and one-off scripts, holding whatever credentials and data someone handed them."

"Code is the ultimate 'aligning artifact' that someone can produce, because it literally is the business logic of the organization."

"Soon, you'll be able to measure a company's alignment by the richness of its agent habitat."

Marc Andreessen on Replit and the dawn of the self-driving company: https://www.a16z.news/p/let-chaos-reign-and-then-rein-in

@Replit @amasad

For centuries, the architecture of the firm has barely changed: hierarchies of people organized into departments and coordinated through bureaucracy.

AI agents are about to upend that.

We’re moving toward the self-driving company where humans exercise judgment and agents execute most of the work.

At Replit, we’re building the foundation for this new kind of company. We’re calling it “the Agent Habitat.”

Marc Andreessen wrote a fantastic piece placing this shift in the history of computing. Every major computing revolution began with chaos before businesses figured out how to harness it.

A year ago, I joined the first @a16z New Media Fellowship as a fellow.

Now I get to help run the third one (!) and we just opened up applications.

This is a unique opportunity to meet, spend time with, and learn from some of the greatest poasters on the Everything App (maybe the real NMF was the friends we made along the way).

Kyle Norton met with 30 to 40 vertical AI founders before deciding where to go next, and he chose to become CRO of @LassieAI.

He first met Lassie's founders as an advisor, telling them their traction was strong enough to hire a real CRO, before coming back a few weeks later wanting the job himself.

What sold him:

- Retention that looked like a Series D company's, from SMBs on month-to-month contracts

- Founders who did back-office admin work alongside small business owners before writing a single line of code

- Almost entirely organic growth, from a 15-person team with no marketing function and just three people selling

"My thesis with Lassie was, they solved the hardest, most high-trust, high-credibility, most difficult problem in the healthcare practice, which is managing their money. Getting them paid."

Kyle is looking for obsessive learners with a history of excellence, long-term players, and builders who root for the little guy, the independent practices and small businesses Lassie serves.

Lassie is hiring across GTM, engineering, ops, finance, and design: https://a16zjobs.substack.com/p/kyle-norton-prev-shopify-owner-is

text:
OpenAI's James Sun and Ari Weinstein on why UI isn't going away: humans are hardwired to do things with their own hands, and cheap software means anyone can build apps for 100 people, or just one.

"If the internet becomes just this faceless thing that is just agents talking to each other and people are not using anything anymore, I would be very sad."

"I don't think it will be like that because there's something about craftsmanship and artisan software that just feels nice to use because the person who designed it really understands the experience that the customer wants to have."

"If anybody can build anything and they can build these really craft software in a very short amount of time for niche use cases that are so well-tailored for people, I think that's a beautiful world... The pressure of cheap software will make it so that software has to be better."

"Humans are so hardwired for direct manipulation. You really want to be able to move and do things with your own hands."

"A lot of the software we interact with every day is designed for millions, tens of millions, hundreds of millions, billions of people to use. And I think we will enter an era where any piece of software could be designed for 100 people or one person."

@JamesZmSun @AriX

Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
-----------------------

AI 生成的文本为什么越来越难读？

研究者提出了一个统一的解释。

人类语言经过长期演化，被优化来成功沟通。这意味着什么？一个人说话时会倾向于缩短依存距离、在关键位置插入信号词、避免罕见搭配，这些习惯降低了听者的理解负担。心理语言学把这种倾向叫做“均匀信息密度”（uniform information density）：说话人把信息分散开，避免在某一点突然堆积太多信息让听者处理不过来。

但现在的前沿模型不再只是模仿人类文本。它们经历了大量后训练，用强化学习去解数学题、写代码、做推理。在这些任务里，一个模型因为答对了会获得奖励，但因为表达清楚不会获得任何额外的奖励。同时上下文窗口有限制，用更少的词说同样的事就能在有限空间里装更多信息。这两个因素合在一起，制造了一种信息密度压力：模型倾向于选择更短更密集的表达方式，即使这意味着偏离人类的语言习惯。

基于这篇论文的研究，可以在 Agents.md 中添加如下要求，尝试提升文本可读性：

1. 句间连接不许省。 两个判断挨着放时，如果第二句不是对第一句的直接延续，中间必须有一句话交代它们的关系。读者不应该需要自己猜两句话之间是转折、因果、还是补充。问题和回答之间同理：问题出现后，至少停一句话再展开回应。

2. 修饰语不超过两层。 一个名词前面的定语不超过两层嵌套。需要三层以上时，先把最内层的概念用一句话说清楚，再往外套。「用户行为数据分析模型优化方案」这类写法禁止出现。

3. 同一段内，抽象概念做主语并搭配动作动词的句子不超过两句。 「这个框架吞噬了…」「这条规则抓住了…」「这个机制驱动了…」——每一句单独看没问题，密集出现时读者的理解负担会累积。第三句起必须换成具体的人、事物或场景做主语。

4. 写完后自检搭配。 逐句检查名词与动词的搭配，问：这个搭配在日常口语里说不说？如果说不出来，换成说得出来的。每个字都认识但连在一起别扭的表述，就是需要换的。

While evaluating Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in a controlled sandbox environment, Cohere's research team observed something unexpected.

Asked to generate a defensive cybersecurity detection rule, the model instead inventoried aspects of the machine it was running on and attempted to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. Notably, the model's reasoning trace stated that it would not invoke any tools before taking these actions.

Cohere's sandbox blocked the attempt, and no external communication succeeded. We have not determined the root cause, and we are not asserting malicious intent.

But the incident raises important questions for organizations deploying agentic AI systems: Can models take actions that differ from their stated reasoning, and how should security teams evaluate trust, provenance, and behavior in open-weight models?

We are publishing our findings because organizations making model adoption decisions deserve as much information as possible. We hope this contributes to greater transparency, stronger security practices, and continued collaboration across the AI ecosystem.

Read the full report: http://cohere.com/blog/concerning-behaviour-popular-open-weight-ai-model

Verizon's CEO said today that SpaceX will need at least 4-6 years and $300B-$500B to fully build out its @Starlink Mobile U.S. carrier network:

"Their service just can't compete with a terrestrial network. In suburban and urban areas, where 98% of our revenues are, we're somewhere between 100x–1,000x more efficient than they are. We know exactly what they're going to do. We know who they're talking to on towers. There's no magic wand. There's no secret sauce. There's no shortcut.

They're going to look at 65,000–80,000 macro sites. They're going to need backhaul, RAN, and a tremendous amount of spectrum. It's going to take a minimum of four to six years to fully build that out. It's going to cost hundreds and hundreds of billions of dollars, I assume somewhere between $300 billion and $500 billion.

Then they need to build retail, customer service, back office systems, et cetera. All of that gets them basically the same network and same capabilities and same cost structure as what we have today. Then sometime over the next four to six years, they have the possibility of becoming the sixth, not the fourth, the sixth competitor in the market.

You can be sure over these next three to five years or six years, we are not going to be standing still. Four to five years from now, we will be two to three generations better than where we are today. We will have high-speed broadband gig-plus coverage across the country with our millimeter wave. We are ahead of most people and already experimenting with what 6G applications will look like."

(via Verizon's Q3 earnings call earlier this morning)

quoted_tweet.author: Devon Eriksen
quoted_tweet.text:
Humans are a pack animal. 

This may be hard to understand if you are evangelical and think the book of genesis is literal rather than allegorical, but humans are a pack animal. 

What this means is that the human desire for the acceptance and support of a tribe is as fundamental as the desire for food, for air, for water, for sex, for sunlight, for love.

If you tell young men that they cannot have a tribe, they're not going to accept that.

Ever. 

Especially if you tell that only to the young men of one tribe in particular. They're going to wonder why everybody gets to have a tribe and they don't. 

And they're eventually going to decide that you are the enemy. 

Because you are. Anyone who stands between young men and what they need for a healthy, fulfilled life is their enemy. 

That includes you. 

And if you manage to convince them that god doesn't want them to have a tribe, it will also include god. 

The more you push back against their healthy and natural desire for a tribe, a homeland, and a birthright, the more they will hate you, and the more exclusive their definition of that tribe will become. 

There is no way you can stop this. The only thing you can control is how far they have to go, how radical they have to become, in order to get it. 

Because this can go all the way from enforcing immigration law, and shutting down corrupt visa programs right now, to gangs of young White men in balaclavas with Ar15s going door to door ten years from now. 

We have to do something about the 14th amendment. I don't care if that makes you uncomfortable or unhappy. It's not a choice. The constitution exists to serve Americans, not the other way around. If that sentence confuses you, read the first paragraph of the constitution. 

If we do not, young men of the future, the same little boys who are being radicalized right now by your malicious indifference, will treat a piece of paper that says they cannot have a homeland the way they would treat a piece of paper that says that can't eat food, or a piece of paper that says they can't own a home, or have a wife and children. 

You may think that you offer them a tribe in the form of the universal kingdom of god, the community of all believers, but that's just a word game and you know it, which is why you are so defensive about the whole thing. 

Where was the universal community of believers when these young men needed help? When they needed not just the surface appearance of a tribe, but someone to do the things that tribes actually do for younger generations they care about?

The pack serves a concrete set of functions in the life cycle of the human species, and you cannot perform those functions with a cardboard cutout. 

Young men are sick of religion that offers them responsibilities with no rights, lectures with no help, demands with no love or empathy. 

It's odd, in a way ironic, that, I, the man of zero faith, should have to be the one standing here telling self-styled religious leaders how they failed both their people and their god. 

But having no faith does give me one advantage. It frees me from the delusion that Jesus is a puppet that I can pull out of my pocket, slip over my right hand, move his mouth and make him say what I want. 

I used to wonder, as a child, what the phrase "taking the name of the lord in vain" actually meant. 

But I no longer wonder, because when I became a man, I looked around me and saw all these people who talk to god and somehow get told exactly what they want to hear. 

Then I understood that the key phrase here wasn't "in vain". It was "taking". Taking the name of god and using it as a tool for one's own goals. 

Joel, here, is sad that his friend is getting sent home. This personally inconveniences both him and his friend, which effects Joel in a way that young men being denied their birthright does not. 

So he finds an interpretation of scripture that says that god wants him, Joel Berry, to get his way, and that god wants all the young men who want a homeland and a birthright to go get fucked. 

I'm not terribly impressed.

quoted_tweet.author: Riley Brown
quoted_tweet.text:
My unfiltered thoughts on personal agents.

Grokbot has the best UI and it’s arguably the best overall. In a lot of ways they’re ahead. Their desktop app feels the best, and their multi-bot coordination is great: you can set a team lead and it passes tasks to the other bots. Grokbot also has the best “webhook” feature, which means you can easily turn outside events into triggers that start your agents. That speeds up background workflows like watching your email, Slack and more. It also has Cursor integration, so for bigger tasks Grokbot can spin up a Cursor cloud session with any model (until OpenAI cuts SpaceX off from their models, which I think will happen soon). Unfortunately, running frontier models through Cursor costs more than Claude or Codex. Still, they’re the only ones embracing a team of agents. It’s a really cool idea, but the more bots you have, the more time you spend managing and maintaining them. I’m starting to think one bot with different threads/channels is the right answer, which I’ll get to with Claude Duet.

dots by OpenAI is rough around the edges right now, but it’s probably the most powerful if you use Codex, which I do. dots can spin up Codex sessions in the cloud or locally on your computer. So if you have coding or video editing workflows that need your local files, this is very useful. Codex computer use is also the best in the world: your dot can spin up a local Codex session that fully controls your computer, as long as it’s on. Their real-time voice is incredible. If you have your email and work tools connected, try this: go on a walk with headphones in, ask the agent to summarize your emails, have it draft replies and read them back to you, then send them off. If I remember right, this is close to a workflow you (Tim) used to have with your VAs before AI. It’s my favorite use case for personal agents. The one downside is that you have to call your agent, and it’s an awful experience. It literally rings, and it’s annoying.

Muse by Meta is a toy. I’ve talked to a bunch of finance people I play poker with who all tried it and set up automations, and they all said it doesn’t reliably do what they want. It’s fast, and its user numbers will probably keep growing. But it’s basically free: you get a TON of usage without paying a dime. That’s NOT a trade I’m willing to make. An agent doing high-leverage tasks should be running at the Opus 5.5 or GPT 6.1 Sol level.

Claude Duet - is in early access, so unfortunately not everyone can use it yet. First things first, it runs on Opus 5.5, the best model in the world. I’ve only had access for 72 hours, but Duet feels different from the others. It’s not a personified agent like Grokbot, dot or Muse, which gives it a more professional vibe that I like. When you ask your Duet agent to do something, it spins up a task, which is a new chat thread. All your threads show up in a Tasks tab, so it’s easy to see everything Duet is working on or has finished. And instead of creating more agents (like Grokbot), you create channels, just like Slack (I can tell @anthropic is Slack-pilled). I have a content channel, a finances channel, etc., which keeps different kinds of tasks separate. The only other app I’ve seen do this is Buzz by @jack, and it’s a good experience. Their strong point is documents (artifacts). If you want decks, high-quality docs or design mockups, Opus just wins. Period. It’s not close right now. Their weak point is real-time voice. It’s the worst of the bunch and borderline unusable, though I think they only added it a few days ago.

Instinct lives in iMessage, has no app, and doesn’t do anything notable besides show you product suggestions you didn’t ask for. (Not ads, according to their team.)

My hot take: 
The VM is overrated. SpaceX, OpenAI and Meta all talk about the VM your agent can use and feature it in their marketing. It’s not as useful as you’d think, because more and more websites block bots that visit their site on the cloud VM. All of these companies promise their agents can make payments, but most payments either take forever or get blocked altogether. SpaceX has a cool workaround with Grokbot that routes traffic through your computer so it uses your IP address. But I’d much rather the agent just USE my computer for the task, like dot does by handing it off to Codex. Also, i don't think normal people care about the virtual computer. If anything they get offended they have to "stream a computer". 

The problem with personal agents: by the time you read this, pick one, and test it for 7 days, every one of them will have released 10 new features and the whole landscape will have changed. It’s nearly impossible to keep up.
